title: How to Survive Email Overload
author: Luca Foppoli
summary: This issue of The Intentional Manager, written by Luca Foppoli with a co-author known as Renato, asks how a manager can protect limited mental bandwidth from the daily flood of email. It opens from the premise that every email forces task switching and that open problems keep consuming capacity until they are closed. Renato explains why Inbox Zero failed him (an empty inbox but a full head) and describes sorting email by problem, killing five-to-ten-minute items immediately, and capping work in progress at his capacity in a kanban style. Luca grounds his own method in the Zeigarnik effect, arguing that a concrete plan is enough to let the brain release an unfinished task, so he assigns every email an action, an owner and a due date and then reviews the list weekly. The two systems differ in temperament, one built on owning problems until solved and the other on classifying them and forgetting them until due, yet both treat attention as the scarce resource a leader must guard. The closing advice is to pick the system that fits your own brain and start it this week.
points: Inbox Zero clears the screen but not the mind, because for managers most emails are deep problems that stay open in the head until they are actually solved.
Renato's method is to kill small items on the spot, delegate or trash the rest, and give important items a backlog slot only up to his capacity, so that nothing new starts until something closes.
Luca's method rests on the Zeigarnik effect: assigning an action, an owner and a due date to each email lets the brain stop holding it open without the problem being solved.
A weekly review of due items and pending replies is what makes either system trustworthy enough to let the mind rest.
The shared lesson for leaders is that attention is finite, so the system should match how your own brain handles unresolved work.
quotes: Information goes around through emails, and each email forces continuous task switching, fragmenting focus and ultimately reducing the amount of mental bandwidth available for solving the actual problem.
Then I closed the laptop and kept chewing on every damn thing I’d just fiddled with in the inbox. Empty inbox, full head.
The important items get a slot on my backlog in order of priority up to my capacity, and nothing new starts until something closes. Stop starting, start finishing.
My answer to this problem stems from a fundamental consideration: your brain is a processing machine, not a filing cabinet.
I “solve” emails as soon as I read them, by assigning an action, an owner and a due date.
The point is to classify the email, so my brain can stop keeping it open in the background - the problem itself can wait.

Then I forget the project update exists at all, until it pops up on Thursday, which is when I have planned a two-hour slot to write it. Until then? Non-existent in my brain and not a single thought spared.
Pick the system that fits your brain and start this week: the next 392 billion emails are already on their way.
